doc.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012

title: How he makes a living: gigs, charts and Finale since moving to New York
summary: Income was nearly all gigs and touring in Chicago until 2006; in New York he adds charts, arrangements, radio and vocalists.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Present day, if you look at your — I’m leapfrogging here — but if you’re doing your taxes at the end of the year and you’re looking at how you make a living, is it mostly from playing gigs and touring? Does selling CDs come into it? Does writing charts? And how is it divided up for you. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Since I moved to New York I write a lot more charts because I finally broke down and got the music transcription software — I use Finale. I should learn Sibelius it’s similar. I should know them both. But I would say when I was living in Chicago, until 2006, I was playing, I would say that 99.9 percent of my income came from playing gigs and touring. And now, in New York, where there’s 80 million crazy ways to make money as a musician, I’ll play for a vocalist, I’ll write out charts for someone, I’ll write out arrangements for someone, I’ll do a radio show. You never know. So now, when I do my tax return, as you say, I look at it and I kind of smile thinking oh when did I find time to do all this stuff. This is great. And your resume builds. And I’m happy about that because I end up learning — playing for singers is something that a lot of instrumentalists, particularly piano players, think oh jeez do I have to do this. But I enjoy it, because I always learn new tunes. For example if I’m doing a gig with a vocalist who’s doing 22 numbers, sometimes I have to learn 14 of them. Good. About time. Sometimes you need to get your butt kicked to learn new music and there’s no more dramatic way of being compelled to learn new music is the gig Saturday you’ve got to have charts ready to go for the band.
